title: Dot products and weighted sums
goals: Calculate a dot product by matching feature positions
Explain how a weight changes a score with other inputs fixed
Distinguish a weighted score from a probability or trained model

prerequisite.prompt: Under schema [width, height], why must [4, 2] and [2, 4] remain distinct?
prerequisite.answer: Their components assign different values to width and height. A calculation using different weights for those features can produce different results.

vocabulary: A numerical coefficient multiplying one input component
The sum of products of corresponding vector components
The product of one input component and its matching weight
A numerical output whose interpretation must be specified

lesson.title: Match a weight to each input

blocks.text: A small model can combine several measurements into one score. Let x = [4, 2] contain fictional width and height measurements in cm. Set weights w = [2, -1]. Multiply matching positions, then add: s = (2 times 4) + (-1 times 2) = 6. The letter x names the input vector.

We call this calculation a dot product, written w dot x. The vectors must have the same number of components. Each weight belongs to one named feature. These hand-selected weights demonstrate a computation; no training has happened. The result 6 is a score, not a probability or a claim that this parcel is safe.
The coefficients carry score-per-cm units in this example, making both contributions compatible score units. A weighted sum needs a consistent definition of units.

lesson.title: Compare inputs with a fixed computation

blocks.text: Keep w = [2, -1] fixed. For A = [4, 2], the score is 6. For B = [2, 4], it is 4 - 4 = 0. For C = [3, 3], it is 6 - 3 = 3. Swapping input positions without swapping their matching weights changes the computation. A zero score can come from cancellation, even when neither input is zero.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The length check matters: Python zip alone stops at the shorter list and could silently omit a feature. The function assumes numeric inputs already validated under the schema. First predict the three printed values on paper, then compare.

blocks.title: Multiply matching components then add
blocks.caption: The first two rows are separate contributions. The last row combines them; multiplying the final input sum by the final weight sum would be a different operation.

blocks.label: Keep w = [2, -1]. Change [4, 2] to [4, 3]. Compute both contributions and explain the score change.

blocks.text: Holding other inputs fixed, raising width by 1 cm raises this score by 2; raising height by 1 cm lowers it by 1. A negative weight reverses the direction of that feature contribution. It does not label the feature as bad, and its sign alone does not explain cause in the world.

Unit changes affect coefficients. If height is written in mm instead of cm while width remains in cm, use height weight -0.1 instead of -1 to preserve the same scores. For [4 cm, 20 mm], 2 times 4 plus -0.1 times 20 still gives 6. Raw coefficient magnitudes cannot establish feature importance when units differ.

A weighted sum can combine evidence, but it discards information: [4, 2] and [5, 4] both produce score 6 under these weights. A downstream rule receiving only that score cannot recover which of these vectors was used. To classify, we would also need a stated decision rule and labelled evaluation examples.

blocks.label: A teammate calls score 6 a 60 percent chance of class 1. What is missing from that claim?

blocks.text: Next week adds an offset called a bias and states exactly how a score becomes a class prediction.

workbook.title: Calculate contributions
workbook.prompt: For w = [2, -1] and x = [3, 5], write both contributions and their sum.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions are 6 and -5, so the score is 1.

workbook.title: Explain cancellation
workbook.prompt: For w = [2, -1] and x = [2, 4], explain why score zero does not mean the input contains no information.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions 4 and -4 cancel. The input still contains width 2 and height 4; zero is the combined score.

workbook.title: Preserve a unit change
workbook.prompt: Width stays in cm and height changes to mm. For the worked parcel [4 cm, 20 mm], give the revised weights and score.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Use [2, -0.1]. Contributions 8 and -2 give score 6, preserving the original measurement meaning.

workbook.title: Compute a new dot product independently
workbook.prompt: Use x = [3, 1, 2] and w = [-2, 4, 0.5]. Give each contribution and the total. Increase only the second component from 1 to 2 and compute the new total. Explain why a two-weight list is invalid for this input.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Contributions -6, 4, 1 give -1. With second component 2, contributions -6, 8, 1 give 3, a rise of 4. Three input components need three matching weights; silently dropping the final component changes the computation.

workbook.title: Find lost information
workbook.prompt: Verify that [4, 2] and [5, 4] both score 6 with w = [2, -1]. Can a later step receiving only this score distinguish those two records?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The scores are 8 - 2 = 6 and 10 - 4 = 6. A deterministic later step receiving only 6 receives identical information and cannot distinguish them.

teacher.background: Teach the dot product as a traceable sum of signed contributions in two 45-minute sessions. Keep weights fixed throughout each comparison and separate hand-chosen parameters from training. Students should explain a score change using the corresponding coefficient, while retaining the limits of that interpretation.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Ask the prerequisite question. Check signed multiplication with -1 times 2 before introducing a dot product.
Lay out the contribution table. Students draw a connection between each named input and its own weight.
Complete W1 and W2. Trace A, B and C with the same weights; discuss cancellation rather than calling zero an empty input.
Run or trace the guarded Python function. Try a missing weight and explain the error. Complete the guided change.
Retrieve the two contributions for A. Ask what changes if height increases while width stays fixed.
Complete W3, converting only height to mm. Show why weight magnitude depends on units.
Collect W4 independently. Require the three signed contributions, original and changed totals, and the dimension error explanation.
Complete W5 and the exit response. Use the fresh retry after targeted feedback; keep first attempts for assessment.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: [4, 3] gives 8 and -3, total 5, down 1 from 6 because height rose by 1 with coefficient -1. Exit: the score has no supplied probability mapping, fitted probability model or calibration evidence. Multiplying it by ten does not create a supported probability.
misconceptions: The operation is 2 times 4 plus -1 times 2, not (2 - 1) times (4 + 2). That shortcut happens to match for some inputs but is not the rule.
A negative coefficient changes direction. Units, data and the rest of the model affect interpretation.
These values were supplied. Training would require data, an objective and a fitting procedure.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires contributions -6, 4, 1 and total -1, changed total 3 and a dimension check. Fresh retry: w = [1, -3, 2], x = [2, 1, 4] gives 2 - 3 + 8 = 7. If only the third input falls to 3, the score is 5. Ask for the two-point decrease explanation.
teacher.support: Provide three labelled contribution boxes and a number line for signed addition. Extension: permute both inputs and matching weights together and show that the sum is preserved; then permute only one to expose a schema mismatch.
teacher.next: Week 3 adds a bias after the dot product and uses an explicit decision boundary.
